parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a restrictive national border/document regime with a strongly protective division. Universal national exposures dominate: sex-binary passport/visa rules, cable instructions to refuse cases where documents cast doubt on sex, possible fraud-based lifetime ineligibility, blocked X markers, foreign travel advisories, airport scanner/pat-down outing, a federal single-sex facilities ban, and documented hostile practices in immigration and corrections custody. Inside the division, documented operative protections — public-accommodations and employment bans since 2006, gender-identity hate-crime penalties, panic-defence repeal, shield-law care access for visitors, gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms, 'Most Protective' ranking — mitigate everyday exposure. Imprisonment or worse is not a credible outcome here, but border refusal, stranding, and custody harm keep the score out of Reduced Risk.

entry_documents.exposure: Feb 2025 end of X markers and self-selection; Nov 2025 Supreme Court allowed restrictions; cable instructs refusal where documents cast doubt on sex and consideration of fraud-based lifetime ineligibility; travellers report blocked/confiscated passports; foreign governments issued advisories. Universal border exposure.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports valid until expiry; fraud finding requires four elements with limited waiver and is never automatic; policy challenged in national courts; legal-aid FAQ on document rules.
entry_documents.interaction: Border refusal/secondary inspection can escalate into detention, where national custody practices apply regardless of division protections.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style policies for trans inmates (hair cutting, hormone removal); trans immigration detainees report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; prisoner counts no longer reported.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National hate-crime statute and division's functional courts provide theoretical recourse; several executive orders enjoined.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visitor detained over document discrepancies enters this custody system; division protections do not govern federal custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Jan 2025 executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide, including federal buildings and airports; 21+ state/provinces have facility bans, 4 criminalise in certain circumstances (one arrest documented elsewhere).
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has no facility ban; single-occupancy public restrooms gender-neutral since 2020; largest city requires no proof for bathroom access; sits in 'Most Protective' tier.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal facility exclusion still operates inside the division at federally funded sites, so local protection is incomplete.

care_services.exposure: National orders target gender-affirming care framing, funding freezes, and proposed insurance bars for under-18s; DOJ subpoenaed under-19 patient records.
care_services.protection: Division shield law (2023) protects patients and providers, explicitly covering people travelling from outside the division to obtain care; public insurance covers surgery 21+; conversion therapy on minors banned.
care_services.interaction: Shield law materially protects a visiting adult or travelling family seeking care, though its resilience to out-of-division subpoenas is uncertain.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: DOJ memoranda and May 2026 counterterrorism strategy use 'radical gender ideology' framing; EO directs law enforcement to investigate 'gender ideology' in schools; 66% of public support ASAB listing on documents; advocates invoke genocide-stage comparisons.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Reward criterion is not trans status; strategy states counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement; division's equality laws and human-rights enforcement counter locally.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National framing raises the temperature at border and in hostile states, but operates weakly inside the protective division.

minors_guardians.exposure: EO threatens criminal prosecution of teachers facilitating social transition; youth-care bans in 27 state/provinces; proposed federal insurance bars for under-18 care; 4 state/provinces flagged Do-Not-Travel.
minors_guardians.protection: Division bans youth conversion therapy, prohibits gender-identity bullying, protects care via shield law covering out-of-jurisdiction families, and has inclusive school policies in its largest city.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling parent and minor are protected within the division but revert to national custody/entry rules at the border and in federal facilities.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National hate-crime statistics show sustained bias incidents; only 23 state/provinces cover gender identity in bias-crime statutes; one documented bathroom arrest (handcuffed, held in men's ward) occurred in another state.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division: gender-identity hate-crime penalties since 2016, gay/trans panic defence repealed 2017, public-accommodations ban since 2006, sodomy decriminalised since 1962.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: In-division recourse is real; travel elsewhere in the country strips these protections.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Key national measures unresolved or enjoined, so exposure varies by travel date; hate-crime prosecution data, shield-law durability, and implementation of the 2024 out-of-state birth-certificate provision are not sourced.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Active ACLU litigation, legal-aid FAQs, functioning division courts, long-standing equality enforcement, and a July 2026 'Most Protective' ranking.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Litigation creates volatility: outcomes could improve or worsen the border regime without local action.

anchor_checks.comparison: Higher than 0.35-A. That anchor is a routine, unreviewable entry register barring all transgender visitors. Here refusal is instructed but conditioned on document discrepancy or suspected misrepresentation, requires four fraud elements with waiver, is under active litigation, and only governs the border stage. Inside the division, documented protections and working remedies have no counterpart in 0.35-A.

Close overall, but split. The border regime is harsher than 0.55-B: mandatory marker rules, refusal instructions, possible lifetime ineligibility, and documented custody abuse exceed discretionary secondary screening with administrative refusal. The division's in-country position — 20-year equality enforcement, hate-crime penalties, shield-law care — is materially safer than 0.55-B's slow, rarely-revised remedies.

Lower than 0.75-C. There border officers are trained, respectful, with a tribunal hearing appeals, counsel access and compensation for unlawful holding. Here the operative cable directs refusal on sex doubt, contemplates lifetime fraud findings, and multiple governments have issued travel advisories; documented federal custody abuses have no analogue in 0.75-C.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets two systems. At the border, the national regime is the binding exposure: sex-binary document rules, instructed refusal on sex doubt, fraud-based lifetime ineligibility exposure, lost X markers, foreign advisories, scanner outing, and — if detained — documented abusive federal custody. No division law touches these. Once inside, the division inverts the picture: two decades of operative equality enforcement, gender-identity hate-crime penalties, panic-defence repeal, gender-neutral facilities, and a shield law expressly covering visiting patients and families. Federal single-sex facility bans still apply at federally funded sites, and litigation volatility means the border rules could shift before travel. Imprisonment for being trans is not a credible in-division outcome, but entry refusal, stranding, and custody risk cap the score below Reduced Risk.
